x: We have already explained the interpretation of the words of God Almighty, Alif, Lam, Meem.
The translators of the Qur’an differed in their interpretation of the words of God Almighty: Alif, Lam, Meem.
Some of them said: It is one of the names of the Qur’an.
Those who said that mentioned:

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement: Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: It is one of the names of the Qur’an.

c: Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim Al-Amili told me: Abu Hudhayfah Musa bin Masʿud told us: Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an.

c: Al-Qasim bin Al-Hasan told us: Al-Hussein bin Dawud told us: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an.

x: Some of them said: They are opening verses with which God opens the Quran.
Those who said this were:

c: Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm al-Kufi told me: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Maharbi told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem are opening verses with which God opens the Qur’an.

c: Ahmad bin Hazim Al-Ghafari told us: Abu Naim told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem are opening letters.

c: Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Yahya bin Adam, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Ibn Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem, Alif, Muḥammad, and Sad are the opening letters with which God began.

c: Al-Qasim bin Al-Hasan told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: like the hadith of Harun bin Idris.

x: Others said: It is the name of the Surah.
Those who said this are:

c: Yunus bin Abdul A’la told me, he said: Abdullah bin Wahb told us, he said:
m: I asked Abdul Rahman bin Zaid bin Aslam about the words of God: “Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book,” and “Alif, Lam, Meem. This is a revelation,” and “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the name of the chapters.” He said: My father said: They are only the names of the chapters.

x: Some of them said: It is the greatest name of God.
Those who said this are:

c: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi told us: Shu’bah told us:
m: I asked al-Suddi about Ha Meem, “Ta Seen Meem,” and Alif Lam Meem. He said: Ibn Abbas said: They are the greatest name of God.

c: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Abu al-Nu’man told us: Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Ismail al-Suddi, on the authority of Murrah al-Hamadani, who said: Abdullah said:
m: He mentioned something similar.

c: Al-Muthanna told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ubaidullah bin Musa, on the authority of Ismail, on the authority of Al-Sha’bi, who said:
m: The openings of the surahs are among the names of God.

x: Some of them said: It is an oath by which God swears, and it is one of His names.
Those who said this were:

c: Yahya bin Othman bin Saleh Al-Sahmi told me, he said: Abdullah bin Saleh told us, he said: Muawiyah bin Saleh told me, on the authority of Ali bin Abi Talha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said:
m: It is an oath by which God swears, and it is one of the names of God.

c: Yaqub bin Ibrahim told us: Ibn Ulayyah told us: Khalid Al-Hadha’ told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, who said:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem is an oath.

x: Some of them said: It is a collection of letters separated from nouns and verbs, each letter having a meaning different from the meaning of the other letter.
Those who said this are:

c: Abu Kurayb told us, he said: Wakiʿ told us, and Sufyan ibn Wakiʿ told us, he said: My father told us, on the authority of Sharik, on the authority of Ataʿ ibn al-Saʿib, on the authority of Abu al-Dhaha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: Alif, Lam, Meem. He said: I, God, know best.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Abu Ubaid,
m: who said: Abu Al-Yaqzan narrated to us, on the authority of Ata’ bin Al-Sa’ib, on the authority of Sa’id bin Jubayr, who said: His statement, Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: I, God, know best.

c: Musa bin Harun Al-Hamdani told me: Amr bin Hammad Al-Qannad told us: Asbat bin Nasr told us, on the authority of Ismail Al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, on the authority of Abu Malik, and on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and on the authority of Murrah Al-Hamdani, on the authority of Ibn Masoud, and on the authority of some of the companions of the Prophet,
m: may God bless him and grant him peace: Alif, Lam, Meem. He said: As for Alif, Lam, Meem, it is a letter derived from the letters of the spelling of the names of God, may His praise be exalted. Surat Luqman 31:1 Alif, Lam, Meem Muhammad ibn Muammar told us:
b.via: some of the companions of the Prophet

c: Abbas ibn Ziyad al-Bahili told us: Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Abu Bishr, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: regarding His statement: Alif, Lam, Meem, “Ha, Meem,” and Nun, he said: It is a disconnected noun.

x: Some of them said that they are letters of the alphabet that were placed.
Those who said that were mentioned:

c: It was narrated on the authority of Mansur ibn Abi Nuwayrah,
m: who said: Abu Saeed al-Mu'addab narrated to us, on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: The opening letters of all the surahs, Qaf, "Sad, Ha Meem, Ta Seen Meem, Alif Lam Ra," and others, are a fabricated spelling.

x: Some of them said: They are letters, each of which includes various different meanings.
Those who said that were mentioned:

c: Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim Al-Tabari told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Abdullah bin Abi Jaafar Al-Razi, who said: My father told me, on the authority of Al-Rabi bin Anas,
m: regarding the statement of God, the Most High: Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: These letters, from the twenty-nine letters, are spoken by all tongues. There is not a letter among them that is not a key to one of His names. There is not a letter among them that is not related to His favors and trials, and there is not a letter among them that is not related to the duration of a people and their appointed times. Jesus, son of Mary, said: And it is strange that they speak of His names and live in His provision, so how can they deny Him? He said: The Alif is the key to His name: God, the Lam is the key to His name: Latif, and the Mim is the key to His name: Majeed. The Alif is the favors of God, the Lam is His kindness, and the Mim is His glory. The Alif is years, the Lam is thirty years, and the Mim is forty years.

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Abu Jaʿfar, on the authority of Al-Rabiʿ,
m: something similar.

x: Some of them said: These are letters from the abjad numeral system. We were reluctant to mention the one who narrated this, as the one who narrated it was someone whose narration and transmission were not reliable. A similar narration has already been reported from Al-Rabi' ibn Anas.
Some of them said: Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur’an is its openings. As for the Arabists, they differed about the meaning of that.

Some of them said: They are letters from the alphabetical letters, and mentioning what was mentioned of them at the beginnings of the surahs dispensed with mentioning the rest of them, which are the completion of the twenty-eight letters, just as the informant dispensed with mentioning what he reported that there are twenty-eight letters in the alphabet by mentioning A B T Th, without mentioning the rest of its letters, which are the completion of the twenty-eight. He said: Therefore, that book was raised, because the meaning of the speech is: Alif, Lam, and Mim are from the separate letters, that is the book which I have revealed to you all together, there is no doubt about it.
A B T Th has become like a noun in the letters of the alphabet, just as Al-Hamd was the name of the Opening of the Book.

Since it was permissible for a speaker to say: My son is in Ṭā Ḍaḥ, and it was known from his saying that if he said it that he wanted to report about his son that he was in the disconnected letters, it was known from that that Ṭā Ḍaḥdoes not have a name, even if that was more effective in mentioning than the rest of them.

He said: The difference between mentioning the letters of the alphabet in the openings of the surahs is that they are mentioned at their beginnings differently, and they are mentioned when they are mentioned at their beginnings, which are A B T Th, together, in order to separate the report about them if what is meant by mentioning what is mentioned from them differently is to indicate connected speech and if what is meant by mentioning what is mentioned from them together is to indicate the separate letters specifically. And they cited as evidence for the permissibility of the saying of the speaker: My son in T Z and the like, from the report about it that it is in the letters of the alphabet, and that this is from his saying in the statement that it takes the place of his saying: My son in A B T Th in the rajaz of some of the rajaz poets of Banu Asad:
h
When I saw her matter in Hatti

and I joked about her lying and flattery I took from her the horns of the Shamat, and she has not left me with her and her giving Even the head was covered with blood He claimed that he meant by that the report about the woman that she was in Abu Jad, so he made his statement:
h
When I saw her matter in Hatti
, in place of his report about her that she was in Abu Jad, since that was from his statement, indicating to his listener what his statement: When I saw her matter in Abu Jad indicates to him.

Others said: Rather, it was started with this at the beginning of the surahs to open the ears of the polytheists to listening to it, as they had advised each other to turn away from the Qur’an, so that when they listened to it, the composition of it would be recited to them.
Some of them said: The letters that open the Surahs are letters with which God opens His speech.
Is there anything in the Qur’an that has no meaning?
The meaning of this is that he began with it to indicate that the surah before it had ended, and that he had begun another, so he made this a sign of the break between them.

This is in the speech of the Arabs, when a man among them recites poetry and says: But, a town whose people are not human He says: No, it did not stir up sorrows and grief But it is not from the verse and is not counted in its meter, but it is used to interrupt a sentence and start another.

Each of the statements made by those whose statement we have described in this regard has a known basis. As for those who said: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an, there are two aspects to their statement: One: That they meant that "Alif, Lam, Meem is the name of the Qur'an, just as Al-Furqan" is its name. If the meaning of the speaker is thus, then the interpretation of his statement, "Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book," is to mean an oath. It is as if he said: By the Qur'an, this Book, there is no doubt about it. The other of them: That they meant that it is one of the names of the surah by which it is known, just as all other things are known by their names which have signs by which they are known. So the listener understands from the speaker saying: Today I read Al-Muddaththir and Al-Nun, meaning the surahs that he read from the surahs of the Qur’an, just as he understands from him if he says: Today I met Amr and Zayd, and they know by Zayd and Amr what he met from the people.

If the meaning of this is unclear to someone, he may say: How can this be so, when there are a number of surahs similar to alif, lam, meem and alif, lam-ra in the Qur’an? Names are only indicators if they distinguish between people, but if they are not distinguishing, then they are not indicators. It has been said: Although the names have become, due to the commonality of many people in one of them, not distinctive except by other meanings with it, such as adding the relation of the named to it, or its description or attribute, in a way that distinguishes it from other forms of it, they were initially established for distinction, no doubt. Then, when there is a need for the meanings that distinguish between those named by them. Likewise, in the names of the surahs, each name, according to the one who said this, was made an indication of the surah named by it. So, since the named shares in it other surahs of the Qur’an, the one reporting a surah from it needed to add to its name the named by it something that would differentiate the hearer between reporting about it and others, of a description, attribute, or other than that.

So the one reporting about himself says that he recited Surat Al-Baqarah, if he calls it by its name, which is Alif, Lam, Meem: I read Alif, Lam, Meem, Al-Baqarah. And in Al Imran 3:I read Alif, Lam, Meem, Al Imran. And “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the Book.” "And "And, 'Alif, Lam, Mim. God, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining." It is as if he wanted to inform about two men, each of whose name was Amr, except that one of them was Tamimi and the other Azdi, he would have to say to the one he wanted to inform about them: I met Amr al-Tamimi and Amr al-Azdi, since there is no difference between them and others who share their names, except their lineage. This is also the case with those who interpret the disconnected letters as names of surahs. As for those who said: These are openings with which God Almighty begins His speech, they directed that to something similar to the meaning we narrated from the one we narrated that from among the Arabs, that he said: These are evidence of the end of a surah and the beginning of another, and a sign of the interruption of what is between them, just as you made rather at the beginning of a poem an indication of the beginning of it and the end of another before it.

Just as we mentioned about the Arabs, when they wanted to begin reciting a poem, they would say: Rather, what stirred up sorrows and grief had been grief. But it is not from the house nor is it included in its meter, but it is used to indicate the end of one speech and the beginning of another.

These are disconnected letters, some of which are names of God Almighty, and some of which are attributes of Him, and each letter has a meaning other than the meaning of the other letter, then they interpreted this in a manner similar to the poet’s saying: We said to her: Stand for us. She said: Stand. Don't think that we forgot to stand.

Meaning by his saying: Qalata Qaf, she said: I have stopped. So by making the Qaf pronounced from Waqafa, she indicated what she meant by the completion of the word in which she stopped. So they diverted his saying Alif, Lam, Meem and the like to something like this meaning.

Some of them said: The Alif is the Alif of Ana, the Lam is the Lam of God, and the Meem is the Meem of A’lam, and each letter of them indicates a complete word. They said: So the sum of these disconnected letters, if they appear with each letter of them, completes the letters of the word, Ana, God A’lam. They said: And likewise all that is at the beginning of the chapters of the Qur’an from that, so based on this meaning and this interpretation, they said: It is widespread and apparent in the speech of the Arabs that the speaker among them reduces letters from the word, if what remains indicates what was deleted from it and adds to it what is not from it, if the addition does not confuse its meaning to its listener, like their deletion in the reduction of the Tha’ from Harith, so they say Ya Har, and from Malik the Kaf, so they say Ya Mal, and the like, and like the saying of their rajaz poet: What is wrong with the oppressed?

How can he not save his skin if he does not? As if he wanted to say: If he does such and such, he was satisfied with the letter ya from yaf’ala, and as another of them said: Good things come to you, and evil things come to you. He wants: evil. I don't want evil unless you He wants: unless you wish, so he was satisfied with the ta’ and the fa’ in both words, from the rest of their letters, and other similar examples that would take too Surat Luqman 31:1 Alif, Lam, Meem long to cover in the book.

c: And as Yaqub bin Ibrahim told me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah told us, on the authority of Ayoub and Ibn Awn, on the authority of Muhammad, he said:
m: When Yazid bin Muawiyah died, Abda said to me: I do not see it except as a trial, so flee from your estate and join your family. I said: What do you command me? He said: I would prefer for you to... Ayoub and Ibn Awn said, with his hand under his right cheek, describing lying down until you see a matter that you recognize.

x: He meant by Ṭadtajiʿu, so he sufficed with the Ṭadtajiʿu from Ṭadtajiʿu. And as the other said in the addition to the statement, in the manner that I described: I say, when you fell on the hump, O my camel, you have not traveled far He wants: all of it, and as the other said: My shape and your shape are different, so stick to the short ones and lower your whites So he added a letter Ḍād, but it is not in the word. They said: Likewise, what is missing from the complete letters of each of these words that we mentioned is the completion of the letters Alif-Lam-Meem and its counterparts is similar to what is missing from the speech that we narrated from the Arabs in their poetry and speech. As for those who said: Every letter of alif-laam-meem and its counterparts indicates various meanings, like what we mentioned from Ar-Rabi’ ibn Anas, they explained that to the same interpretation as he explained to him who said: It is based on the interpretation God knows best, in that every letter of it is some of the letters of a complete word, and its indication of its completeness suffices without mentioning its completeness, even though they disagreed with him regarding every letter of that: Is it from the word that the proponents of the first opinion claimed it was from, or from another one?

They said: Rather, the alif of alif-laam-meem is from various words, and it indicates the meanings of all of that and its completeness. They said: Each letter of that was isolated, and was limited by it to completing the letters of the word, because if all of the letters of the word were made clear, the word that is made clear, in which some of these disconnected letters are some, would only indicate one meaning, not two meanings or more than that. They said: Since there is no indication in that, if all of them were made clear, except for their meaning, which is a single meaning, and since God, the Most High, intended to indicate with each letter many meanings for one thing, it is not permissible except to isolate the letter indicating those meanings, so that those addressed by it know that God, the Mighty and Sublime, did not intend to intend one meaning and indicate one thing with what He addressed them with, and that He only intended to indicate many things with it.

They said: The Alif in Alif, Lam, Meem implies many meanings, including the completion of the name of the Lord, which is God, and the completion of the name of God’s blessings, which are His favors, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is one year, since the Alif in the abjad system is one. The Lam implies the completion of the name of God, which is Latif, and the completion of the name of His bounty, which is Lutf, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is thirty years. The Mim implies the completion of the name of God, which is Majestic, and the completion of the name of His Greatness, which is Majestic, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is forty years. The meaning of the speech, according to the interpretation of those who say the first opinion, is that God, may He be glorified and exalted, began His speech by describing Himself as the All-Knowing from whom nothing is hidden, and He made that a method for His servants to follow at the beginning of their sermons, letters, and affairs, and a test from Him for them so that they may deserve a great reward in the abode of recompense, just as He began with Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth (al-An’am 6:1), and other similar surahs whose openings He made praise of Himself, and just as He made the openings of some of them glorifying and venerating Himself with praise, as He, may He be glorified and exalted, said: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night (al-Isra’ 17:1), and other similar surahs of the Qur’an, the openings of some of which He made praising Himself, the openings of some of which glorifying Him, and the openings of some of which glorifying and sanctifying Him.

Likewise, He made the keys to the other surahs, which begin with some letters of the alphabet, praises of Himself, sometimes with knowledge, sometimes with justice and fairness, and sometimes with generosity and kindness, in brief and concise terms, then the matters are summarized after that. According to this interpretation, the alif, lam, and mim in the places of the nominative case should be raised by each other, without his saying that book, and that book would be a predicate subject separate from the meaning of alif, lam, mim. Likewise, that in the interpretation of the statement of the one who says this second statement, is raised by each other, even if its meaning is different from the meaning of the statement of the one who says the first statement. As for those who said: They are letters from the letters of the abjad calculation without any meanings that contradict that, they said: We do not know of any meaning for the disconnected letters that can be understood other than the abjad calculation, and other than the spelling of the saying of the speaker: Alif, Lam, Meem.

They said: It is not permissible for God, the Most High, to address His servants except in a way that they understand and comprehend. Since that is the case and His saying Alif, Lam, Meem does not have a rational face that could be directed to it, except one of the two faces that we mentioned, then one of its faces is invalidated, which is that it is intended by it to spell Alif, Lam, Meem. It is correct and proven that it is intended by it to mean the second face, which is the abjad calculation, because the saying of the speaker: Alif, Lam, Meem cannot be followed by the statement That is the Book, because the meaning of the statement is impossible and goes beyond reason, if “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the Book” follows it.
They also argued for their statement with the following:

c: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me: al-Kalbi narrated to me, on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Ri’ab, who said:
m: “Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, while he was reciting the opening verse of Surat al-Baqarah 2:‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book about which there is no doubt.’ So his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab from the Jews came and said: ‘By God, you know that I heard Muhammad reciting, in what God, the Almighty, revealed to him, ‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book.’ They said: Did you hear it? He said: ‘Yes!’ So Huyayy ibn Akhtab walked with those Jews to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and they said: ‘O Muhammad, was it not mentioned to us that you recite, in what was revealed to you, ‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book.’ The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Yes.’ They said: ‘Did Gabriel bring this to you from God?’ He said: ‘Yes.’ They said: God, the Almighty, has sent prophets before you, and we do not know of any prophet among them who explained what…’” His reign was prolonged and his nation did not eat except you! So Huyayy ibn Akhtab said, and he turned to those who were with him and said to them: The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Mim is forty, so that is seventy-one years. Will you enter the religion of a prophet whose reign and nation did not eat except for seventy-one years? He said: Then he turned to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: O Muhammad, is there anything else with this? He said: Yes. He said: What? He said: Alif-Lam-Meem. He said: This is heavier and longer. The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, the Mim is forty, and the Sad is ninety, so that is one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything else with this, O Muhammad? He said: Yes. He said: What? He said: Alif-Lam-Ra. He said: By God, this is heavier and longer. The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Ra is two hundred, so that is two hundred and thirty-one years. He said: Is there anything else with this, O Muhammad? He said: Yes, al-murr. He said: By God, this is heavier and longer. The alif is one, the lam is thirty, the mim is forty, and the ra is two hundred. This is two hundred and seventy-one years. Then he said: Your matter has become so confusing to us, O Muhammad, that we do not know whether you have been given a little or a lot. Then they got up from him. Abu Yasir said to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the rabbis who were with him: How do you know? Perhaps he has gathered all of this for Muhammad: seventy-one, sixty-one and one hundred, two hundred and thirty-one, two hundred and seventy-one. That is seven hundred and thirty-four years! They said: His matter has become confusing to us! They claim that these verses were revealed about them: “It is He who has sent down to you, [O Muhammad], the Book. In it are verses that are precise - they are the foundation of the Book - and others unspecific.”
r
(Al Imran 3:7)

They said: This report clearly proves the correctness of what we have said about this interpretation, and the corruption of what our opponents have said about it. The correct statement in my opinion about the interpretation of the keys to the Surahs, which are the letters of the alphabet, is that God, the Most High, made them separate letters and did not connect some of them to others, making them like all other speech with connected letters, because He, the Most High, intended by His wording to indicate with each letter many meanings, not just one meaning, as Ar-Rabi’ ibn Anas said. Even though Ar-Rabi’ limited it to three meanings, without anything more than that. The correct interpretation of this, in my opinion, is that each letter of it contains what Al-Rabi’ said, and what all other commentators have said about it, except for what I mentioned from the people of Arabic who I mentioned: that he directed the interpretation of this to that they are letters of the alphabet. Mentioning what he mentioned of it in the keys to the surahs suffices, without mentioning the rest of the twenty-eight letters of the alphabet, by interpreting: that these letters, that book, are collected, there is no doubt about it, for it is a false and corrupt statement, as it departs from the statements of all the companions and followers and those who came after them from the dissenters of the people of interpretation and exegesis. So it is sufficient to indicate his error, the testimony of the proof against him of the error, with the invalidation of the one who said that, as we have narrated from him, when he turned to explaining the raising of that book by saying once that each one of them is raised by its companion, and another time that it is raised by the referent of what he mentioned in his saying there is no doubt about it, and once by his saying a guidance for the righteous. This is an omission from him, based on his statement that alif, lam, mim is the subject of that book, and a departure from the statement he claimed in the interpretation of “alif, lam, mim. That book,” and that the interpretation of that is: these letters are that book.

q.l: If someone were to say to us:
x: How can one letter be comprehensive in indicating many different meanings?

Just as it is possible for a single word to include many different meanings, such as their saying for a group of al-Nas 114:a nation, and for a particular moment in time: a nation, and for a devout and obedient man: a nation, and for religion and creed: a groan. And like their saying for recompense and retaliation: a religion, and for authority and obedience: a religion, and for humiliation: a religion, and for accountability: a religion, and there are many similar things that would take a long time to list, as speech is made with one word, and it includes many meanings. And likewise the statement of God, may He be praised: Alif, Lam, Meem, “Alif, Lam, Ra,” Alif, Lam, Meem, and what is similar to that from the letters of the alphabet which are the opening letters of the surahs, each letter of which denotes various meanings, encompassing all of them from the names and attributes of God, the Almighty, as the commentators have said from the sayings we have mentioned. And they are, however, the opening letters of the surahs, as those who have said so have said. And the fact that these are from the letters of the names and attributes of God, may He be praised, does not prevent them from being opening letters for the surahs.

Because God, may He be glorified and praised, has opened many chapters of the Qur’an with praise and thanks to Himself, and Surat Luqman 31:1 Alif, Lam, Meem many of them with glorification and exaltation of Him, so it is not impossible that some of them begin with an oath by Him. As for the ones whose opening letters begin with the letters of the alphabet, one of the meanings of their opening letters is that they are the opening letters of the chapters of the Qur’an. They are among what God swore by, because one of their meanings is that they are letters of the names and attributes of God, the Most High, as we have explained previously. There is no doubt that the meaning of swearing by God, His names and attributes is correct. They are among the letters of the abjad system. They are symbols and names for the chapters that begin with them. This encompasses the meanings of all that we have described, from what we have explained, from its aspects.

Because if God, the Most High, had intended by this, or part of it, to indicate a single meaning from what it could bear, without all other meanings, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would have made that clear to them. This is because God, the Most High, only revealed His Book to His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, to clarify to them what they differed about. And in the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, not explaining that, that some of its interpretations are intended by it and not others, is the clearest evidence that it is intended by all of its aspects for which it is possible. It was not impossible in the mind for any of them to be from its interpretation and meaning, just as it was not impossible for the many meanings of one word to come together, in one expression, in one statement. Whoever rejects what we have said about this should be asked about the difference between this and other letters that have a single pronunciation, yet contain many different meanings, such as nation, religion, and similar nouns and verbs.

He will not say anything about one of these without necessarily saying the same thing about the other. Likewise, anyone who interprets any of these things in a way that is different from the other ways we have described should be asked about the proof for his claim, from the way that must be accepted. Then he should counter with the statement of his opponent on this matter, and ask about the difference between them: from the origin, or from what the origin indicates. So he will not say one statement without requiring the same in the other.

i: As for the grammarians who claimed that this is similar to the saying of the poet:
x: Rather, what stirred up sorrows and grief had been grief.

And that it has no meaning, but rather it is an addition to the speech whose meaning is to throw it away, so he made a mistake in many ways: One of them is that he described God Almighty as having addressed the Arabs in a language other than their own, nor in the language of any human being. Although the Arabs used to begin their poetry with bal, it is known that they never began any of their speech with alif, lam, meem, “alif, ra,” or alif, mas, in the sense of beginning it with bal. And since that was not part of their beginning, and God Almighty only addressed them with what He addressed them from the Qur’an, with what they knew of their languages and what they used among themselves of their speech, in every verse, then there is no doubt that the path of what we have described of the letters of the alphabet, with which the beginnings of the surahs, which are openings, is the path of the rest of the Qur’an, in that He did not deviate with them from the languages they knew and used among themselves in their speech.

Because if this was deviated from the path of their languages and logic, it would be outside the meaning of clarification with which God, the Almighty, described the Qur’an, when He, the Most High, said:
The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue

How can something be made clear that no one in the world can comprehend or understand, according to the statement of the one who said this statement, and that is not known in the language of any of the created beings, according to his statement? And in God’s statement that it is a clear Arabic, there is what belies this statement, and indicates that the Arabs were knowledgeable about it, and it is clear to them. This is one of the aspects of his error. The second aspect of his error in this regard is that by attributing it to God, the Most High, He addressed His servants with something that has no benefit or meaning for them, through speech in which it is the same to address them with it or not to address them with it.

This is by attributing the futility that is denied in the words of all monotheists about God to God, the Most High. The third aspect of his error is that bal in the speech of the Arabs has an interpretation and meaning, and that they include it in their speech to return to a statement that has already been completed, like their saying: It was not your brother who came to me, but rather your father, and I did not see Omar, but rather Abdullah, and similar statements, as A’sha of Banu Tha’labah said: And I will drink eight, eight, thirteen, two, and four. He continued his speech until he said: In the sitting, and the goodness of his arms is like a balloon that hits me like a finger Then he said: Rather, count this, in another verse, and mention a young man of generous nature, the most wonderful. It is as if he said: Leave this and take up another style of poetry. Rather, it only comes in the speech of the Arabs in this manner of speech.

As for opening their speech with a beginning meaning of length and deletion, without indicating a meaning, that is something that we do not know of anyone who has claimed from the people of knowledge of the Arabic language and its logic, except for the one whose statement you mentioned. So that would be a principle by which the letters of the dictionary, which are the openings of the chapters of the Qur’an that were opened with it, could be likened if they were similar to it, so how is it that it is far from resembling it?

evidence.text: Others said: Rather, it was started with this at the beginning of the surahs to open the ears of the polytheists to listening to it, as they had advised each other to turn away from the Qur’an, so that when they listened to it, the composition of it would be recited to them.

x: Those who establish prayer means: those who establish the obligatory prayer within its limits. And give zakat means: those for whom God has made it obligatory from their wealth. And they are certain of the Hereafter. He means: they do that and they are certain of God's reward and recompense for whoever does that in the Hereafter.

God Almighty says: These are the ones whose characteristics have been described in clear terms from their Lord and in light. And it is they who are the successful ones. The people of interpretation differed in their interpretation of His statement,
h
And among the people is he who buys the amusement of speech
Some of them said: He who buys the known purchase for a price, and they narrated a report about that from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.

c: This is what Abu Kurayb told us.

He buys the one who is idle talk, or the one who is idle talk, so he is buying idle talk. As for the hadith, the people of interpretation differed about it.
Some of them said: It is singing and listening to it.

c: Yunus ibn Abd al-A’la told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Yazid ibn Yunus told me, on the authority of Abu Sakhr, on the authority of Abu Mu’awiyah al-Bajali, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Abi al-Sahba’ al-Bakri,

x: God Almighty says, Indeed, those who have believed in God, made Him One, believed in His Messenger and followed him, and done righteous deeds meaning, they obeyed God, did what He commanded them in His Book and on the tongue of His Messenger, and refrained from what He forbade them from, for them are gardens of pleasure meaning, to these people are orchards of pleasure.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: Muadh ibn Muadh told us, on the authority of Imran ibn Hudayr, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:

m: He created the heavens without pillars that you can see. He said: Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They are without pillars that you can see, they do not have pillars. Ibn Abbas said: Without pillars that you see. He said: It has pillars that you do not see. His statement,

And He has placed firm mountains on the earth

, lest it should move with you, means: He placed firm mountains on the back of the earth, lest it should move with you, that it not move with you. He says: that it not shake with you, nor move to the right or to the left, but that it remains still for you.

m: And He has cast into the earth firm mountains: meaning mountains lest it should move with you He fixed it with the mountains, and were it not for that, He would not have established a creation upon it, and that is as the rajaz poet said. And We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow therein every kind of noble pair

This is the creation of God

So they are in error. He says: They are in injustice toward the truth and in manifest deviation from the straight path. He says: It is clear to whoever contemplates it, looks into it and thinks with reason that it is misguidance and not guidance.

x: God Almighty says: And We gave Luqman understanding of religion, reason, and correct speech. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us,
m: both of them, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, his statement,
h
And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom
, means understanding, reason, and correctness of speech, without prophethood.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom
, meaning understanding of Islam. Qatada said: He was not a prophet, and revelation was not sent to him.

c: Yaqub bin Ibrahim told me, he said: Hisham told us, he said: Yunus told us, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom
, he said: Wisdom means correctness.

x: Others than Abu Bishr said: Correctness is other than prophecy.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us, on the authority of Muhammad Ibn Jaʿfar, who said: Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of Al-Hakam, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Luqman was a righteous man, but he was not a prophet.

c: Nasr bin Abdul Rahman Al-Awdi and Ibn Hamid told me: Hakam told us, on the authority of Saeed Al-Zubaidi, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Luqman the Wise was an Ethiopian slave, with thick lips and smooth feet, and he was a judge over the Children of Israel.

c: Isa bin Othman bin Isa Al-Ramli told me: Yahya bin Isa told us on the authority of Al-A’mash, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: Luqman was a black slave, with thick lips and cracked feet.

c: Abbas bin Muhammad told me, he said: Khalid bin Mukhallad told us, he said: Sulayman bin Bilal told us, he said: Yahya bin Saeed told us, he said:
m: I heard Saeed bin Al-Musayyab say: Luqman the Wise was a black man from the black people of Egypt.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Ash’ath, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said:
m: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave.

c: Al-Abbas bin Al-Walid told us: My father told us: Al-Awza’i told us: Abd Al-Rahman bin Harmalah told us:
m: A black man came to Saeed bin Al-Musayyab asking, so Saeed said to him: Do not be sad because you are black, for three of the best people were black: Bilal, Mahja’, the freed slave of Omar bin Al-Khattab, and Luqman the Wise, who was a black Nubian with long lips. Ibn Wakee’ narrated: My father narrated to us, on the authority of Abu Al-Ashhab, on the authority of Khalid Al-Rab’i, who said: Luqman was an Ethiopian slave who was a carpenter. His master said to him: Slaughter this sheep for us. So he slaughtered it. He said: Take out the two best parts of it. So he took out the tongue and the heart. Then he waited as long as God willed, then he said: Slaughter this sheep for us. So he slaughtered it. He said: Take out the two worst parts of it. So he took out the tongue and the heart. His master said to him: I ordered you to take out the two best parts of it, so you took them out. And I ordered you to take out the two worst parts of it, so you took them out. Luqman said to him: There is nothing better than these two when they are good, and nothing worse than these two when they are bad.

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Al-Hakam told us: Amr ibn Qays told us:
m: Luqman was a black slave with thick lips and smooth feet. A man came to him while he was talking with some people and said to him: Aren’t you the one who used to tend the sheep with me in such and such a place? He said: Yes. He said: What brought you to what he saw? He said: Be truthful in your speech and keep quiet about things that do not concern me.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of a man, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: And We gave Luqman wisdom. He said: The Qur’an. He said: My father told me, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: Wisdom is trustworthiness.

x: Others said: He was a prophet.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told me, on the authority of Israel, on the authority of Jabir, on the authority of Ikrimah, who said:
m: Luqman was a prophet. And His statement,
h
To be grateful
to God, means,
h
And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom
, [saying], ‘To praise God for what He has given you of His bounty.’ He made His statement,
h
To be grateful
, a translation of wisdom, because part of the wisdom that he was given was his gratitude to God for what He had given him. And His statement,
h
And whoever is grateful is only grateful for [the benefit of] himself
, means,
h
And whoever is grateful is only grateful for [the benefit of] himself

, because God will reward him abundantly for his gratitude to Him and save him from destruction. And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed, God is Free of need and Praiseworthy, means, “And whoever is ungrateful for God’s favor upon him, has wronged himself, because God will punish him for his ingratitude to Him. God is Free of need of his gratitude to Him for His favors, and He has no need of them, because his gratitude to Him does not increase His power, nor does his ingratitude to Him decrease His kingdom.” And by His statement, Praiseworthy, He means, Praiseworthy in every situation, to whom praise is due for His favors, whether the servant is ungrateful for His favor or grateful to Him for it.” And it is changed from a passive participle to a passive participle.

x: God Almighty says to His Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace: And remember, O Muhammad, “when Luqman said to his son while he was advising him, ‘O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is a great wrong.’” He says: A great mistake in speech.
God Almighty says: And We have commanded man to be dutiful to his parents.
h
His mother bore him with weakness upon weakness

. He says: weakness upon weakness, and hardship upon hardship. From this is the saying of Zuhair: They will not say that a weak rope was created. If your people had been in its causes, they would have perished.
The people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that, but they differed about the meaning of that.
Some of them said: It means pregnancy.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: regarding His statement, “
h
And We have enjoined upon man
, concerning his parents. His mother carried him, with weakness upon weakness,” meaning: hardship after hardship, and creation after creation.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say: Regarding His statement,
h
And here upon weakness
, he said: Weakness upon weakness.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: his statement,
h
His mother bore him with weakness upon weakness
, meaning effort upon effort.

x: Others said: Rather, what he meant by it is the weakness and frailty of the child due to the weakness of the mother.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us
m: both, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
h
And here upon weakness
, he said: It is the child upon the weakness and frailty of the mother. His statement,
h
And his weaning is in two years
, means: And his weaning is at the end of two years. It was also said,
h
And his weaning is in two years
, and he omitted mentioning the end of two years, as the statement indicates it, just as it was said, And ask the town in which we were
r
(Yusuf 12:82)
, meaning the people of the town. His statement,
h
That you be grateful to Me and to your parents

, means: We have enjoined upon you to be grateful to Me for My blessings upon you, and to your parents for raising you and treating you with the hardship they endured until you attained maturity. His statement,
h
To Me is the final destination

, means: To God is your final destination, O human being. He will ask you about your gratitude to Him for His blessings upon you, and about your gratitude to your parents and your dutifulness to them for the suffering and hardship they endured from you during your childhood and youth, and about their dutifulness to you and their compassion toward you. He mentioned that this verse was revealed regarding Saad bin Abi Waqqas and his mother. Mentioning the narration mentioned in that:

c: Hannad bin Al-Sarri narrated to us: Abu Al-Ahwas narrated to us, on the authority of Samak bin Harb, on the authority of Musʿab bin Saʿd, who said:
m: Umm Saʿd swore that she would not eat or drink until Saʿd converted from his religion. He said: But he refused, and she remained like that until she fainted. He said: Then her sons came to her and gave her something to drink. He said: When she came to, she invoked God against him, and this verse was revealed:
h
And We have enjoined upon man
, concerning his parents ... until His saying: in this world, [doing] good.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us: Muhammad bin Jaʿfar told us: Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of Samak bin Harb, on the authority of Musʿab bin Saʿd, on the authority of his father, who said:
m: Umm Saʿd said to Saʿd: Has not God commanded righteousness? By God, I will not eat food or drink anything until I die or you give up. He said: Whenever they wanted to feed her, they would close her mouth with a stick, then they would pull her out. Then this verse was revealed:
h
And We have enjoined upon man
, concerning his parents, good treatment.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us: Abd Al-A’la told us: Dawud told us, on the authority of Samak bin Harb, who said: Sa’d bin Malik said:
m: This verse was revealed regarding, But if they endeavor to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them but accompany them in [this] world with appropriate kindness. He said: When I became Muslim, my mother swore that she would not eat any food or drink anything. He said: I appealed to her on the first day, but she refused and was patient. On the second day, I appealed to her, but she refused. On the third day, I appealed to her, but she refused. So I said: By Surat Luqman 31:14
h
And We have enjoined upon man
, concerning his parents - his mother carried him with hardship upon hardship, and his weaning and gestation are thirty months - [that] he be grateful to Me and to your parents.
h
To Me is the final destination
. God, if you had a hundred souls, you would leave before I abandon this religion of mine. When she saw that and knew that I would not do it, she ate.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us: Muhammad bin Jaʿfar told us: Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, who said:
m: I heard Abu Hubayrah say: This verse was revealed about Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas: But if they endeavor to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them... the verse.

x: God the Most High says: “And if your parents strive to make you, O man, associate with Me in your worship of Me someone other than Me, of whom you do not know that I have a partner, nor does He have a partner - exalted is He, the Most High, far above all - then do not give in to them what they want you to do of associating partners with Me. “And accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness.” He says: And accompany them in this world by obeying them in that for which there is no responsibility upon you between you and your Lord and no sin. And His statement:
h
And follow the way of him who turns back to Me

. He says: And follow the way of he who repents from his polytheism, returns to Islam, and follows Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. And the people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that.
Who said that?

c: Bishr told me, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: And follow the path of him who turns to Me: meaning, of him who comes to Me. And His statement,
h
To Me is your return

, and I will inform you of what you used to do, means that your final destination and return after your death is to Me, and I will inform you of all the good and evil that you did in this world, then I will reward you for your deeds, the good among you for his good deeds, and the evildoer for his evil deeds.

x: If someone were to say to us: What is the point of interrupting this statement between the report of my advice to his son Luqman? We would also say that even if it was a report from God, the Most High, about His advice to His servants, and that He only advised his son Luqman about it, then the meaning of the statement would be: “And when Luqman said to his son while he was admonishing him, ‘O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is great injustice.’” “And do not obey your parents in associating anything with Him. “And accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness.” For God had advised them, so the statement was resumed in the form of a report from God, and this meaning is in it. So that is the point of interrupting it between the two reports about His advice.
Arabists differed about the meaning of the ha' and alif in the phrase it is.
Some of the grammarians of Basra said: This is a metaphor for disobedience and sin. The meaning of the statement according to him is:
h
O my son
, if the disobedience is the weight of a mustard seed, or if the sin is.

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: This ha' is a pillar. He said: We feminized tak because it means a seed, so he adopted the feminine form for it, as the poet said: And shine with the words that you have broadcasted as the chest of the canal shines with blood The author of this article said: It is permissible to put mithqal in the accusative or nominative case. He said: Whoever puts it in the nominative case puts it in the nominative case with tk. The indefinite noun can have no verb in kana, laysa, and its sisters. Whoever puts it in the accusative case makes it an implied, anonymous noun, like the ha’ in His statement, Innahu, if it is… He said: Similar to it is His statement, For indeed, eyes will not be blind Al-Hajj 22:46. He said: If it were if it were the mithqal of a grain, it would have been correct, and both interpretations would be permissible. As for the author of the first article, putting mithqal in the accusative case in his statement is on the basis that it is the predicate and the completion of kana.

He said: Some of them put it in the nominative case and made it kana, which does not need a predicate. The first of the two opinions is the more correct in my opinion, the second, because God, the Exalted, did not promise His servants that He would fully repay them for their bad deeds without repaying them for their good deeds. So it is said: If a sin is the weight of a mustard seed, God will bring it. Rather, He promised both workers that He will fully repay them for their deeds. If that is the case, then the ha’ in His statement it is is more likely to be a pillar than a metaphor for sin and disobedience. As for the accusative in mithqal, it is because in tak there is an unknown word, and the nominative is because the predicate is implied, as if it was said: if tak is in the place of mithqal of a seed, because indefinite nouns have their predicates implied, then it translates from the place where the mithqal of a seed is.

By his saying, the weight of a mustard seed, he meant the weight of a mustard seed. The interpretation of the statement, then, is: If the matter is the weight of a mustard seed of good or evil that you have done, and it is in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth, God will bring it on the Day of Resurrection, and He will give you its reward in full. And the people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that.
Who said that?

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: his statement,
h
O my son
, if it be the weight of a mustard seed of good or evil. The commentators differed on the meaning of His statement, and it will be in a rock.

x: Some of them said: He meant by it the rock on which the earth is, and this is a statement narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas and others. They said: It is a green rock.
Who said that?

c: Abu Al-Sa’ib told me: Ibn Idris told us, on the authority of Al-A’mash, on the authority of Al-Munhal, on the authority of Abdullah bin Al-Harith, who said:
m: The rock was green on the back of a whale.

c: Musa bin Harun narrated to us, he said: Amr narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, on the authority of Al-Suddi in a report he mentioned on the authority of Abu Malik, on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and on the authority of Marra, on the authority of Abdullah, on the authority of some of the companions of the Prophet,
m: may God bless him and grant him peace: God created the earth on a whale, and the whale is the whale that God mentioned in the Qur’an (Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe) (al-Qalam 68:1), and the whale is in the water, and the water is on the back of a rock, and the rock is on the back of an angel, and the angel is on a rock, and the rock is in the wind, and it is the rock that Luqman mentioned, it is not in the sky, nor on the earth.
b.via: some of the companions of the Prophet

x: Others said: He meant the mountains. They said: The meaning of the statement is: So be in a mountain.
Who said that?

c: Bishr told me, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement, and it will be in a rock: meaning a mountain. His saying,
h
God will bring it forth

, some of them interpreted its meaning to mean that God knows it, and I do not know that he will bring it forth means that He knows it, unless the one who said that meant that Luqman described God with that because God knows His places, and nothing of His places is hidden from Him, so it would be a correct interpretation.

x: Who said that?

c: Ibn Bashar told us: Abd al-Rahman and Yahya told us: Abu Sufyan told us, on the authority of al-Suddi, on the authority of Abu Malik:
m: “Then it will be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth.
h
God will bring it forth
.” He said: God knows it.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: Ibn Mahdi told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Al-Suddi, on the authority of Abu Malik,
m: the same. His saying, Indeed, God is Kind and All-Aware means: God is Kind in extracting the seed from its place, and All-Aware of its place. And the people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that.

x: Who said that?

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: Indeed, God is Kind and Aware: that is, Kind in extracting it and Aware of its place of rest.

x: God Almighty says, informing us of what Luqman said to his son:
h
O my son

, establish prayer within its limits. And enjoin what is right means: and enjoin people to obey God and follow His command. And forbid what is wrong means: and forbid people from disobeying God and committing what He has forbidden. And be patient over what befalls you means: and be patient over what befalls you from people for the sake of God if you enjoin what is right and forbid them from what is wrong, and do not let what befalls you turn you away from that. Indeed, that is of the matters [worthy of] determination means: that is one of the matters that God has commanded out of determination. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said: Who said that?

c: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: regarding his statement,
h
O my son

, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you, he said: Be patient over what befalls you of harm in that. Indeed, that is of the matters [requiring] determination, he said: Indeed, that is of the matters that God has determined, meaning: Of the matters that God has commanded.

x: The reciters differed in their reading of the phrase and do not turn up your noses.
Some of the reciters from Kufa, Medina, and Kufa read it and do not turn up your noses on the pattern of tafa'ala.

Some of the Meccans and most of the reciters from Medina, Kufa, and Basra read it and do not turn up your noses on the pattern of tafa'ala. The correct thing to say about this is that they are two readings, each of which has been recited by scholars of the Qur’an, so whichever one the reciter recites, he is correct. The interpretation of the statement is: And do not turn your face away from the one you are speaking to, out of arrogance and contempt for the one you are speaking to. The origin of the word sa’r is a disease that afflicts camels in their necks or heads until their necks are turned away from their heads, and it is likened to a man who is arrogant towards people. From this is the saying of Amr ibn Hani al-Taghlabi: And when the tyrant turned his cheek, we would stand up for him from his leaning, and they would stand up. The commentators differed in their interpretation of this verse.
Some of them said something similar to what we have said.
Who said that?

c: Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, meaning: Do not be arrogant, so as to belittle the servants of God, and turn your face away from them when they speak to you.

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: his statement,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
means: Do not turn your face away from people out of arrogance.

c: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us
m: both, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, And do not turn your face away, he said: turning away and turning your face away from people.

c: Ali bin Sahl told me: Zaid bin Abi Al-Zarqa told us, on the authority of Jaafar bin Burqan, on the authority of Yazid,
m: regarding this verse,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, he said: If someone speaks to you, turn your face away from him, looking down on him.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: Khalid bin Hayyan Al-Raqi told us, on the authority of Ja’far bin Maymun bin Mihran, who said:
m: It is a man who speaks to another man and turns his face away.

c: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad told us: Muhammad ibn Rabi’ah told us: Abu Makin told us, on the authority of Ikrimah,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, he said: Do not turn your face away.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, meaning: Do not turn away from people, meaning: Turn your face towards people and show good character.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said
m: regarding His statement,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, he said: Turning the cheek away means being arrogant and haughty towards people and belittling them.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Abu Makin, on the authority of Ikrimah, who said:
m: Turning away.

x: Others said: He only forbade him from doing that to someone who was close to him, not out of arrogance.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Wakee’ and Ibn Hamid told us: Jarir told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
. He said: A man has envy between him and his brother, and he sees it and turns away from him.

c: Ibn Bashar told us, he said: Abu Ahmad told us, he said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And do not turn your cheek away from people
, he said: It is the man who has a grudge against his brother and turns away from him.

x: Others said: It is the emphasis.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told me, on the authority of Ja’far al-Razi, on the authority of Mughira, on the authority of Ibrahim, who said:
m: It is the clenching of the jaw.

c: Ibn Bashar told us, he said: Abu Ahmad told us, he said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Al-Mughira, on the authority of Ibrahim, he said:
m: It is the emphasis or the emphasis Al-Tabari is in doubt.

c: Yahya bin Talha told us: Fadil bin Ayyad told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Ibrahim,
m: with a similar narration. And His saying,
h
And do not walk on the earth exultantly
, means: Do not walk on the earth arrogantly. It was also narrated on the authority of Al-Hussein, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say:

c: Ubaid told us,
m: who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say, regarding His statement,
h
And do not walk upon the earth exultantly
, that he said: with arrogance.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement, “
h
And do not turn your cheek toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly
. Indeed, God does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.” He said: He forbade him from being arrogant. His statement, Indeed, God does not like everyone self-deluded, is arrogant and boastful.

c: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us,
m: both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding his statement,
h
Every arrogant boaster
, he said: Arrogant. And his statement, Proud, he said: He enumerates what God has given, but he does not thank God.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in their reading of the phrase and do not turn up your noses.
Some of the reciters from Kufa, Medina, and Kufa read it and do not turn up your noses on the pattern of tafa'ala.
Some of the Meccans and most of the reciters from Medina, Kufa, and Basra read it and do not turn up your noses on the pattern of tafa'ala.
The correct thing to say about this is that they are two readings, each of which has been recited by scholars of the Qur’an, so whichever one the reciter recites, he is correct.

x: He says: Be humble in your walk when you walk, do not be arrogant, and do not rush, but take your time.

The people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about this, except that some of them said: He ordered him to be humble in his walking, and some of them said: He ordered him to stop being quick in it. It was mentioned that he ordered him to be humble in his walk.

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Abu Hamza told us, on the authority of Jabir, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: And be moderate in your walking. He said: Humility.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: And be moderate in your walking. He said: He forbade him from being arrogant.

x: Mention of those who said: He forbade him from speeding.

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Ibn al-Mubarak told us, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Uqbah, on the authority of Yazid ibn Abi Habib,
m: regarding His statement, And be moderate in your pace, he said: from speed. His statement,
h
And lower your voice
, he said: Lower your voice, and make it moderate when you speak.

c: As Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: h
And lower your voice
. He said: He ordered him to be moderate in his voice.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said:

m: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement,

x: God Almighty says, Have you not seen, O people, that God has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens of the sun, moon, stars, and clouds and whatever is on the earth of animals, trees, water, seas, ships, and other benefits? All of this is for your benefit and interests, for your food, sustenance, provisions, and refuge. You enjoy some of all of it and benefit from all of it. And He has bestowed upon you His blessings, both apparent and hidden. The reciters differed in their reading of this.

Some of the Meccans and most of the Kufians read it and He bestowed upon you His blessings as the singular, and they interpreted its meaning to mean Islam, or to mean the testimony that there is no god but God. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read it as Ni’mah as the plural, and they interpreted its meaning to mean the blessings that God has subjected to His servants from what is in the heavens and the earth. They cited as evidence for the correctness of their reading the words grateful for His blessings (al-Nahl 16:121). They said: This is the plural of blessings. The correct statement in our view is that they are two well-known readings among the reciters of the regions, and they have close meanings. This is because blessing may mean a single word, or a group, and group may include a single word. God, the Most High, said:
h
And if you should count the favors of God, you could not enumerate them
so it is known that He did not mean a single blessing.
And He said elsewhere:
h
And he was not among the polytheists grateful for His favors

, so He made them plural. So whichever of the two readings the reciter recites that with, he is correct. Some of those who read it mentioned monotheism, and interpreted it as we mentioned about its readers that they interpret it.

c: Ahmad bin Yusuf told me, he said: Al-Qasim bin Salam told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, he said: Mastour Al-Hana’i told me, on the authority of Hamid Al-Araj, on the authority of Mujahid, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: that he read it And He has bestowed upon you His favor, apparent and hidden, and Islam interpreted it.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Farra’,
m: who said: Sharik bin Abdullah narrated on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that he read blessing as one. He said: If it had been blessings, it would have been a blessing less than a blessing, or a blessing above a blessing the doubt is from Al-Farra’.

c: Abdullah bin Muhammad Al-Zuhri told me, he said: Sufyan told us, he said: Hamid told us, he said:
m: Mujahid recited And He has bestowed upon you His favor, apparent and hidden, he said: There is no god but God.

c: Al-Abbas bin Abi Talib told me, he said: Ibn Abi Bakr told us, on the authority of Shibl, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid And He has bestowed upon you His favor,
m: apparent and hidden, he said: He used to say: It is there is no god but God.

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Hamid Al-A’raj, on the authority of Mujahid And He has bestowed upon you His favor,
m: both apparent and hidden, he said: There is no god but God.
b.via: Mujahid And He has bestowed upon you His favor

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: Ibn Uyaynah told us, on the authority of Hamid Al-A’raj, on the authority of Mujahid, who said:
m: There is no god but God. Ibn Wakee’ narrated: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Isa, on the authority of Qais, on the authority of Ibn Abbas a blessing that is apparent and hidden, he said: There is no god but God. And his saying apparent means: apparent on the tongues in words, and on the bodies and limbs of the body in actions. And his saying and hidden means: and hidden in the hearts in belief and knowledge. And His statement,
h
And among the people is he who disputes about God without knowledge or guidance

, God Almighty says: And among the people is he who disputes about the Oneness of God, and sincere obedience and worship of Him, without knowledge of what he disputes about, nor guidance: He says: Nor a statement with which to clarify the truth of what he says, nor an illuminating book, He says: Nor a revelation from God that brought what he claims, clarifying the truth of his claim.

c: As Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: h
And among the people is he who disputes about God without knowledge or guidance
or an enlightening Book. He has no proof or Book from God.

The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read it as Ni’mah as the plural, and they interpreted its meaning to mean the blessings that God has subjected to His servants from what is in the heavens and the earth.

Ahmad bin Yusuf told me, he said: Al-Qasim bin Salam told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, he said: Mastour Al-Hana’i told me, on the authority of Hamid Al-Araj, on the authority of Mujahid, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that he read it And He has bestowed upon you His favor, apparent and hidden, and Islam interpreted it.

x: God Almighty says: And when it is said to those who dispute about the Oneness of God out of ignorance of the greatness of God: “O people, follow what God has revealed to His Messenger and believe in it, for it distinguishes between those among us who are right and those who are wrong, and separates between those who are astray and those who are guided,” and they say: Rather, we follow the religions that we found our fathers following, for they were people of truth, God Almighty says: Or even if Satan were to invite them by making their evil deeds appear attractive to them, and their following him in their misguidance, and their disbelief in God and their abandonment of following what God has revealed of His Book to His Prophet to the punishment of the Blazing Fire, meaning: the punishment of the blazing fire that is blazing and raging.

God Almighty says: And whoever worships His Face, humbly submitting to Him in worship, acknowledging His divinity, and is a doer of good, meaning: and he is obedient to God in His commands and prohibitions, has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, meaning: he has grasped the most trustworthy end, the end of which he does not fear breaking if he holds on to it. This is an example, and what he means by that is that he has grasped the pleasure of God by submitting to Him and is a doer of good, such that he does not fear the punishment of God on the Day of Resurrection. And the people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Abu al-Sawda’, on the authority of Ja’far ibn Abi al-Mughira, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: And whoever submits his face to God while he is a doer of good has grasped the most trustworthy handhold. He said: There is no god but God. His saying, And to God is the outcome of all matters, means: To God is the outcome of every matter, good and bad, and He is the One who will question its people about it and reward them for it.

x: God Almighty says: And whoever disbelieves in God, let not his disbelief grieve you, nor let your soul be consumed with regret over them, for indeed, their return and destiny on the Day of Resurrection is to Us, and We will inform them of their evil deeds that they did in this world, then We will recompense them for them with their due recompense. Indeed, God is Knowing of that within the breasts. He says: Indeed, God is All-Knowing of what their breasts conceal of disbelief in God and preference for obeying Satan.

And His statement, We grant them enjoyment for a little while, means: We grant them respite in this world for a little while in which they may enjoy themselves. Then We will force them to a severe punishment, means: Then We will bring them, against their will, to a severe punishment, and that is the punishment of the Fire. We seek refuge in God from it, and from any action that brings one closer to it.

God Almighty says: And if you, O Muhammad, ask these polytheists among your people, Who created the heavens and the earth? they will surely say, God. Say, Praise be to God. God Almighty says to His Prophet Muhammad: So if they say that, then say to them, Praise be to God who created that, not to the One who does not create anything and is created. Then God Almighty says, But most of them do not know. He says: Rather, most of these polytheists do not know who is to be praised, and where the place of thanks lies.
And His statement,
h
To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth

, God Almighty says: To God belongs everything in the heavens and the earth, whatever that thing may be, whether an idol or a statue or anything else, whether worshipped or not. Indeed, God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy, meaning: God is the Free of need of the worship of these polytheists, idols and rivals to Him, and anything else from them and from all of His creation, because they are His property and His, and they have a need for Him. The Praiseworthy means the One who is praised for His blessings that He has bestowed upon His creation.
God Almighty says: And if all the trees of the earth were to be turned into pens,
h
and the sea
were to replenish it. He says: The sea has ink. The ha in His statement replenishes it refers to the sea. And His statement:
h
After him will be seven more seas

, the Words of God would not be exhausted. In this statement there is an omission that is dispensed with by the apparent meaning of it, which is that the Word of God is written with those pens and that ink, so those pens would be broken, and that ink would be exhausted, but the Words of God would not be exhausted. And the people of interpretation said something similar to what we said about that.
Who said that?

c: Yaqub told me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah told us, on the authority of Abu Raja’, he said:
m: I asked Al-Hasan about this verse,
h

, he said: If the trees of the earth were pens, and the seas were ink, and God said: Indeed, such and such is part of My affair, and such and such is part of My affair, the water of the seas would be exhausted, and the pens would be broken.

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said: Al-Hakam told us, he said: Amr told us,
m: regarding his statement,
h

, he said: If pens were sharpened
h
and the sea
were ink, and it was written with those pens from it, The Words of God would not be exhausted, even if it were for a period of seven ahraz.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And if all the trees on the earth were pens
h
and the sea

were replenished thereafter by seven more seas, the Words of God would not be exhausted. He said: The polytheists said: This is only speech that is about to be exhausted. He said: If the trees of the land were pens,
h
and the sea

were seven seas, the wonders of my Lord, His wisdom, His creation, and His knowledge, would not be exhausted. It was mentioned that this verse was revealed to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, as a result of an argument that the Jews had with him.
